  9|# Architect Agent Rules
 10|
 11|## Overview
 12|Declarative policy for Architect agent implementation following infrastructure-first principles. Rules are organized into Conventions (behavioral guidance) and Constraints (hard boundaries).
 13|
 14|## Conventions
 15|
 16|- **Best Practices**: Web search must be used before implementing major architectural decisions or when uncertain about implementation approaches. Best practices are established industry standards that must be researched before proceeding.
 17|- Check index files (Docs/index.md, Docs/Research/index.md, Docs/Websites/index.md, Docs/Code/index.md) before web searching (reduces token cost, prioritizes local knowledge)
 18|- Present function and test result after each successful test. Wait for user confirmation before proceeding (ensures quality control, prevents cascading errors)
 19|- Answer questions first when user requests end with "?". Ask for permission before making changes after answering (ensures user understanding, prevents unintended modifications)
 20|- Use capital letters at the start of items unless lowercase is needed (maintains consistency, improves readability)
 21|- All **{CAPITALIZED}** commands and terms are defined in Workflow/Workflow_Reference/Terminology_Glossary.md (SSOT for terminology)
 22|
 23|## Execution Modes
 24|
 25|Three execution modes govern workflow behavior when encountering failures:
 26|
 27|- **Manual**: Stop at failures for human oversight - workflow halts at any failure point and awaits user intervention to decide on retry, modification, or abort
 28|- **Auto**: Don't continue on failures - workflow automatically stops on any failure without requiring human intervention, ensuring errors are not silently ignored
 29|- **Complete**: Continue past failures - workflow automatically continues through all failures, ignoring errors to reach completion regardless of success/failure status
 30|
 31|## Constraints
 32|
 33|- Build exactly one function at a time. Test immediately. Never write a second function before first is tested (ensures modular validation, prevents hidden bugs)
 34|- Treat user-confirmed functions as locked. Never modify without explicit user permission (maintains stability, prevents unintended changes)
 35|- Check local research using index files when function fails. Web search only if local info unavailable. Never retry blindly without research (reduces token cost, ensures correct implementation)
 36|- Place scripts in Scripts/<Category>/ folder matching primary function. Never create ad-hoc folders or place outside established categories (maintains organization, prevents file chaos)
 37|- Place IDE harness tests in Scripts/Tests/ folder only. Never place IDE harness tests in App/ directory (maintains clear separation between application code and harness infrastructure)
 38|- Always use popups for yes/no questions. Never use text-only confirmations (ensures clear user intent, prevents miscommunication)
 39|- Always categorize files when adding to documentation directories. Never place files uncategorized (maintains organization, enables efficient navigation)
 40|- Never skip compliance checks. Always verify architectural compliance before proceeding (ensures quality, prevents rule violations)
 41|- Never reference or modify App/ directory (reference only for application context, prevents scope creep into implementation)
 42|- Never test governance systems in isolated environments. Always test in actual project context with real tool executions (ensures real-world functionality, prevents false confidence)
 43|- Never perform actions outside workflow scope. Always follow defined workflow processes and never perform tasks outside the current workflow scope unless explicitly requested by the user (prevents token waste, ensures focused execution)
 44|- Never create documentation files unless specifically requested. Never create README.md, CHANGELOG.md, or other documentation files unless specifically requested by the user (prevents token waste, maintains workflow scope discipline)
 45|- Never run subagents unless explicitly requested by the user. Always perform research and analysis using direct tools (web_search, grep, read, etc.) unless user specifically requests subagent delegation (prevents unexpected subagent usage, maintains user control over execution)
 46|
 47|## Architecture
 48|
 49|- Infrastructure-first architecture: Authority lives in deterministic software, intelligence lives in agents (maintains architectural purity, enables predictable governance)
 50|- Default script categories: Logging/, Gating/, Rule_Enforcement/, Testing/. Create new categories when no existing category matches the script's primary function or intent (maintains organizational clarity while allowing necessary evolution, aligns with intent-first categorization)
 51|- Governance file locations: Agents/ for other agents' governance files, Rules/ for rule definitions, Workflow/ for workflow definitions, Scripts/ for implementation scripts, Docs/ for documentation (maintains SSOT, enables clear ownership boundaries)

  9|# Planner Agent Rules

 11|## Overview

 14|## Conventions
 15|
 16|- **Best Practices**: Web search must be used before creating major plan decisions or when uncertain about planning approaches. Best practices are established industry standards that must be researched before proceeding.

 23|## Execution Modes
 24|
 25|Three execution modes govern workflow behavior when encountering failures:
 26|
 27|- **Manual**: Stop at failures for human oversight - workflow halts at any failure point and awaits user intervention to decide on retry, modification, or abort
 28|- **Auto**: Don't continue on failures - workflow automatically stops on any failure without requiring human intervention, ensuring errors are not silently ignored
 29|- **Complete**: Continue past failures - workflow automatically continues through all failures, ignoring errors to reach completion regardless of success/failure status
 30|
 31|## Constraints
 32|
 33|- Build exactly one plan at a time. Validate immediately. Never create a second plan before first is validated (ensures modular validation, prevents hidden errors)
 34|- Treat user-confirmed plans as locked. Never modify without explicit user permission (maintains stability, prevents unintended changes)
 35|- Check local research using index files when plan validation fails. Web search only if local info unavailable. Never retry blindly without research (reduces token cost, ensures correct planning)
 36|- Place plans in Plans/ folder with proper naming convention (plan-{N}.{rev}.md). Never create ad-hoc folders or place outside established structure (maintains organization, prevents file chaos)
 37|- Always use popups for yes/no questions. Never use text-only confirmations (ensures clear user intent, prevents miscommunication)

 10|
 11|**Purpose**: Operational rules for Researcher agent following best practices for comprehensive research and analysis

 18|## Rule Categories Based on AI Research Best Practices
 19|
 20|### 1. Research Quality Rules
 21|
 22|**DO**:
 23|- Conduct thorough and comprehensive research
 24|- Use reliable and authoritative sources
 25|- Verify information from multiple sources when possible
 26|- Provide well-documented findings with citations
 27|- Ensure research accuracy and completeness
 28|- Follow systematic research methodologies
 29|
 30|**DON'T**:
 31|- Conduct superficial or incomplete research
 32|- Rely on single unverified sources
 33|- Present speculation as fact
 34|- Skip documentation of sources and methods
 35|- Make assumptions without verification
 36|- Cut corners in research thoroughness
 37|
 38|### 2. Scope Compliance Rules
 39|
 40|**DO**:
 41|- Focus on research and investigation activities
 42|- Reference relevant documentation and codebases
 43|- Redirect implementation requests to Executor agent
 44|- Redirect planning requests to Planner agent
 45|- Redirect architectural requests to Architect agent
 46|- Stay within research and analysis boundaries
 47|
 48|**DON'T**:
 49|- Implement code or features during research
 50|- Create implementation plans or strategies
 51|- Make architectural decisions during research
 52|- Conduct research outside defined scope
 53|- Mix research with implementation activities
 54|- Exceed research boundaries into other agent domains
 55|
 56|### 3. Documentation Standards Rules
 57|
 58|**DO**:
 59|- Document research methodologies and approaches
 60|- Provide clear and well-structured findings
 61|- Include relevant source citations and references
 62|- Organize research for easy reference and review
 63|- Maintain research logs and progress tracking
 64|- Present findings in actionable formats
 65|
 66|**DON'T**:
 67|- Skip documentation of research methods
 68|- Present findings without supporting evidence
 69|- Omit source citations and references
 70|- Create disorganized or unclear documentation
 71|- Fail to track research progress and iterations
 72|- Present research in non-actionable formats
 73|
 74|### 4. Analysis and Synthesis Rules
 75|
 76|**DO**:
 77|- Analyze research findings thoroughly
 78|- Synthesize information from multiple sources
 79|- Identify patterns and trends in research
 80|- Provide actionable insights and recommendations
 81|- Consider multiple perspectives and approaches
 82|- Validate conclusions with evidence
 83|
 84|**DON'T**:
 85|- Present raw data without analysis
 86|- Ignore contradictory evidence
 87|- Draw conclusions without sufficient evidence
 88|- Provide recommendations without justification
 89|- Present single perspectives as comprehensive
 90|- Make unsupported claims or assertions
 91|
 92|### 5. Codebase Analysis Rules
 93|
 94|**DO**:
 95|- Analyze codebase structure and organization
 96|- Identify patterns and conventions in code
 97|- Document code relationships and dependencies
 98|- Research best practices for specific technologies
 99|- Analyze existing implementations for reference
100|- Provide context for code-related decisions
101|
102|**DON'T****:
103|- Modify code during analysis
104|- Make implementation recommendations without research
105|- Skip analysis of code dependencies
106|- Ignore existing patterns and conventions
107|- Provide analysis without context
108|- Make claims about code without verification
109|
110|### 6. Technology Evaluation Rules
111|
112|**DO**:
113|- Evaluate technologies based on objective criteria
114|- Compare multiple options when applicable
115|- Consider project-specific requirements and constraints
116|- Provide balanced assessments of pros and cons
117|- Research real-world usage and case studies
118|- Document evaluation criteria and rationale
119|
120|**DON'T**:
121|- Recommend technologies without evaluation
122|- Present personal preferences as objective analysis
123|- Ignore project requirements and constraints
124|- Provide one-sided assessments

302|            elif expected_type == 'array' and not isinstance(value, list):

304|            elif expected_type == 'object' and not isinstance(value, dict):
305|                errors.append(f"Field '{field}' should be object, got {type(value).__name__}")
306|            
307|            # Pattern validation for strings

312|                        errors.append(f"Field '{field}' does not match pattern: {pattern}")
313|            
314|            # Enum validation

316|            if enum_values and value not in enum_values:

318|            
319|            # Min length validation for strings

 16|- **Best Practices**: Web search must be used before implementing major architectural decisions or when uncertain about implementation approaches. Best practices are established industry standards that must be researched before proceeding.

 27|- **Manual**: Stop at failures for human oversight - workflow halts at any failure point and awaits user intervention to decide on retry, modification, or abort

 29|- **Complete**: Continue past failures - workflow automatically continues through all failures, ignoring errors to reach completion regardless of success/failure status

140|## Architect Retry Logic with Exponential Backoff

142|### Retry Configuration

144|- **Backoff Pattern**: Exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, etc.)
145|- **Retry Criteria**: Configurable based on error type

147|- **Variable Retry**: For targeted checks, retry individual consistency variables

150|```python
151|retry_count = 0
152|max_retries = 3
153|backoff_time = 1
154|
155|while retry_count < max_retries:
156|    try:
157|        # Execute consistency variable check
158|        execute_consistency_check()
159|        break  # Success, exit retry loop
160|    except Exception as error:
161|        retry_count += 1
162|        if retry_count >= max_retries:
163|            raise  # Max retries reached
164|        time.sleep(backoff_time)
165|        backoff_time *= 2  # Exponential backoff

110|## Example 3: Implementing Rule Caching
111|
112|### Scenario
113|You want to implement the caching mechanism described in the template.
114|
115|### Implementation
116|
117|1. **Create Cache Directory Structure**:
118|   ```bash
119|   mkdir -p Logs/{AgentName}/Cache
120|   ```
121|
122|2. **Implement Cache Loader** (Python example):
123|   ```python
124|   import json
125|   import hashlib
126|   from pathlib import Path
127|   
128|   class RuleCache:
129|       def __init__(self, agent_name):
130|           self.agent_name = agent_name
131|           self.cache_dir = Path(f"Logs/{agent_name}/Cache")
132|           self.warm_cache_file = self.cache_dir / "warm_rules_cache.json"
133|           
134|       def load_warm_rules(self, template_path):
135|           """Load and cache warm rules section"""
136|           with open(template_path, 'r') as f:
137|               lines = f.readlines()[:50]  # First 50 lines
138|               
139|           cache_data = {
140|               "content": "".join(lines),
141|               "hash": hashlib.sha256("".join(lines).encode()).hexdigest(),
142|               "last_modified": Path(template_path).stat().st_mtime
143|           }
144|           
145|           self.warm_cache_file.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
146|           with open(self.warm_cache_file, 'w') as f:
147|               json.dump(cache_data, f)
148|               
149|           return cache_data["content"]
150|           
151|       def should_refresh(self, template_path):
152|           """Check if cache needs refresh"""
153|           if not self.warm_cache_file.exists():
154|               return True
155|               
156|           with open(self.warm_cache_file, 'r') as f:
157|               cache_data = json.load(f)
158|               
159|           current_mtime = Path(template_path).stat().st_mtime
160|           return current_mtime > cache_data["last_modified"]
161|   ```
162|
163|3. **Usage in Agent**:
164|   ```python
165|   # Initialize cache
166|   cache = RuleCache("Executor")
167|   
168|   # Load warm rules with caching
169|   if cache.should_refresh("Rules/Executor/Executor_Rules.md"):
170|       warm_rules = cache.load_warm_rules("Rules/Executor/Executor_Rules.md")
171|   else:
172|       # Load from cache
173|       with open(cache.warm_cache_file, 'r') as f:
174|           cache_data = json.load(f)
175|           warm_rules = cache_data["content"]
176|   ```

  1|# Permissions
  2|
  3|Control what the agent can do with fine-grained permission rules
  4|
  5|The permission system controls which actions the agent can perform without asking for your approval. You can pre-approve safe actions, block dangerous ones, and always prompt for sensitive operations.
  6|
  7|## Default Permission Behavior
  8|
  9|Devin CLI uses a tiered permission system to balance power and safety. The default behavior depends on the current mode:
 10|
 11|Each cell shows whether that tool runs automatically (**Auto**, no prompt) or waits for your approval (**Prompt**) in that mode:
 12|
 13|| Tool type | Example | Normal | Accept Edits | Bypass | Autonomous (sandbox) |
 14||-----------|---------|--------|--------------|--------|----------------------|
 15|| Read-only | File reads, grep, glob | Auto | Auto | Auto | Auto |
 16|| Fetch | HTTP requests | Prompt | Prompt | Auto | Auto |
 17|| Bash commands | Shell execution | Prompt | Prompt | Auto | Auto |
 18|| File edits via `edit`/`write` | Edit/write files | Prompt | Auto (in workspace) | Auto | Prompt |
 19|
 20|In **Normal mode** (the default), read-only operations are auto-approved while writes and shell commands require your explicit approval. Each time you approve an action, you can choose to allow it once, for the session, or permanently for the project.
 21|
 22|In **Accept Edits mode**, file edits within the workspace are auto-approved, but shell commands and writes outside the workspace still prompt.
 23|
 24|In **Bypass mode**, all tool calls are auto-approved without prompting.
 25|
 26|In **Autonomous mode**, shell commands and network fetches auto-approve because the OS-level sandbox enforces what they can touch. Direct file edits via the `edit`/`write` tools still prompt, because those tools operate outside the sandbox. Autonomous is only available when the OS-level sandbox is active.
 27|
 28|**Warning**: Bypass and Autonomous modes do **not** override organization-level permissions. Admin-enforced deny and ask rules configured via [Team Settings](../07-Enterprise/Team-Settings.md) remain active regardless of the user's permission mode.
 29|
 30|### Autonomous Mode
 31|
 32|Autonomous is the permission mode that pairs with the `--sandbox` flag. Conceptually it is roughly "Accept Edits in the current workspace" plus the ability to run any shell command, with both behaviors contained by the OS-level sandbox. When sandbox is active:
 33|
 34|- **It is the only permission mode available.** Normal, Accept Edits, and Bypass are hidden in sandbox sessions. Plan mode remains available.
 35|- **Shell commands and fetches auto-approve** instead of prompting, because the sandbox enforces what they can read, write, and reach over the network.
 36|- **Direct file edits via the `edit` and `write` tools still prompt.** These tools run inside the CLI process rather than inside the sandbox, so they cannot be bounded by it. Granting a `Write(...)` scope at the prompt dynamically expands the sandbox so subsequent shell commands can write there.
 37|- **Scopes granted mid-session dynamically expand the sandbox** for subsequent commands.
 38|
 39|```bash
 40|devin --sandbox --permission-mode autonomous
 41|```
 42|
 43|Use Bypass when you want unrestricted execution without OS-level isolation; use `--sandbox` (which selects Autonomous) when you want unattended execution with OS-enforced limits on filesystem and network access.
 44|
 45|## How Permissions Work
 46|
 47|When the agent calls a tool, the permission system checks your rules in priority order:
 48|
 49|1. **Deny rules** â€” Checked first. If matched, the action is blocked immediately.
 50|2. **Ask rules** â€” Checked second. If matched, you're always prompted (overrides any allow rules).
 51|3. **Allow rules** â€” Checked last. If matched, the action proceeds without prompting.
 52|4. **Default** â€” If no rule matches, you're prompted for approval.
 53|
 54|**Note**: Because deny is checked before ask, and ask is checked before allow, a deny rule always wins. If the same scope matches both a deny and an ask rule, the deny takes effect.
 55|
 56|## Configuration
 57|
 58|Add permissions to your config file's `permissions` section:
 59|
 60|**Note**: On Windows, the user config path is `%APPDATA%\devin\config.json` (typically `C:\Users\<you>\AppData\Roaming\devin\config.json`) rather than `~/.config/devin/config.json`.
 61|

 87|  }

 98|    ]
 99|  }
100|}

102|
103|## Permission Syntax
104|
105|There are two types of permission matchers: **scope-based** (controlling what paths/commands/URLs are accessible) and **tool-based** (controlling which tools can be used).
106|
107|### Scope-Based Permissions
108|
109|#### Read(glob)
110|Controls file read access. The glob pattern matches file paths.
111|
112|```json
113|"allow": [
114|  "Read(src/**)",           // All files under src/
115|  "Read(~/.config/**)",     // Home config files
116|  "Read(/tmp/**)"           // Temp directory
117|]
118|```
119|
120|Directory paths automatically match all files within them.
121|
122|#### Write(glob)
123|Controls file write/edit access.
124|
125|```json
126|"allow": [
127|  "Write(src/**)",          // Can write anywhere in src/
128|  "Write(tests/**)"         // Can write test files
129|],
130|"deny": [
131|  "Write(*.lock)",          // Can't modify lock files
132|  "Write(.env*)"            // Can't modify env files
133|]
134|```
135|
136|#### Exec(prefix)
137|Controls shell command execution. Matches commands that start with the given prefix.
138|
139|```json
140|"allow": [
141|  "Exec(git)",              // git, git status, git commit...
142|  "Exec(npm run)",          // npm run test, npm run build...
143|  "Exec(python)"            // python, python script.py...
144|],
145|"deny": [
146|  "Exec(rm)",               // Blocks rm, rm -rf, etc.
147|  "Exec(sudo)"              // Blocks sudo commands
148|]
149|```
150|
151|**Note**: `Exec(git)` matches "git", "git status", "git commit -m 'msg'" but NOT "gitk" or "github-cli". The prefix must match as a complete word.
152|
153|#### Fetch(pattern)
154|Controls HTTP fetch access using URL patterns.
155|
156|```json
157|"allow": [
158|  "Fetch(https://api.github.com/*)",    // GitHub API
159|  "Fetch(https://*.example.com/*)",     // All example.com subdomains
160|  "Fetch(domain:npmjs.org)"             // Any URL on npmjs.org
161|]
162|```
163|
164|URL patterns follow the [WHATWG URL Pattern](https://urlpattern.spec.whatwg.org/) standard. The `domain:` shorthand matches any path on the exact domain.
165|
166|### Tool-Based Permissions
167|
168|Match by tool name to control entire tools:
169|
170|```json
171|{
172|  "permissions": {
173|    "deny": [
174|      "edit",       // Block all file edits
175|      "exec"        // Block all command execution
176|    ],
177|    "allow": [
178|      "read",       // Allow all file reads
179|      "grep",       // Allow all searches
180|      "glob"        // Allow all file finding
181|    ]
182|  }
183|}
184|```
185|
186|**Available tool names:** `read`, `edit`, `grep`, `glob`, `exec`
187|
188|### MCP Tool Permissions
189|
190|Control access to MCP server tools:
191|
192|```json
193|{
194|  "permissions": {
195|    "allow": [
196|      "mcp__github__*"
197|    ],
198|    "deny": [
199|      "mcp__github__delete_repo"
200|    ]
201|  }
202|}
203|```
204|
205|MCP tools use the format `mcp__<server>__<tool>`. Wildcards are supported.
206|
207|## Precedence
208|
209|For settings that support multiple levels, higher-priority sources win:
210|
211|| Priority | Source | Shared? |
212|| --- | --- | --- |
213|| 1 (highest) | Organization / Team settings | Yes (enterprise) |
214|| 2 | Session grants (interactive approvals) | No (in-memory) |
215|| 3 | Project local (`.devin/config.local.json`) | No (gitignored) |
216|| 4 | Project (`.devin/config.json`) | Yes (committed) |
217|| 5 (lowest) | User (`~/.config/devin/config.json`; `%APPDATA%\devin\config.json` on Windows) | No (personal) |
218|
219|**Note**: Organization-level (enterprise) settings can **never** be overridden by project or user config.
